The sides of a square are decreasing in length at a rate of $4\text{ cm/s}.$ At what rate is the area of the square decreasing when the side is $10\,\text{cm}$ long?

The area is decreasing at a rate of
{{field-1}}
${\text{cm}}^{2}/\text{s}.$
worked_solution:
Let $x$ and $A$ be the length of the sides and the area of the square, respectively. We want to find

$$
\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.
$$

The area $A$ is related to side length $x$ by the formula

$$
A={x}^{2}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\cdot 2x.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that each side of the square is decreasing at a rate of $4\,\text{cm/s},$ so we have $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-4.$
Also, when the sides are $10\,\text{cm},$ we have $x=10.$ Substituting this information into the above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=-4\cdot 2(10)=-80{\text{ cm}}^{2}\text{/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the square is decreasing at  $80\,{\text{cm}}^{2}/\text{s}.$
